en: *Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra*, Scroll One.

Regarding whether the vow for bodhicitta has been made: the answer is that it has been made. If one follows this sūtra, because the preceptor asks about the seven obstructions (*saptāvaraṇa*), the subsequent sūtra states:
"When one wishes to receive the precepts, the Dharma Master asks: 'In your present body, have you not...'"
Regarding the commission of the seven heinous crimes:
a Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon those who have committed the seven heinous crimes in their present life.
As for the seven heinous crimes:
Drawing blood from the body of a Buddha;
killing one's father, mother, preceptor, or ācārya.
If one has committed the seven obstructions, such as causing a schism in the Saṃgha by disrupting its formal acts (karmavācanā), turning back the wheel of the Dharma, or killing an arhat.
One does not receive the precepts in this very body; all others may receive them.
Yet, the Yoga [Śāstra] says:
The reason for not mentioning the seven obstructions is that one may still obtain the precepts even after performing repentance;
this is unlike the case of a śrāvaka who, having committed a pārājika offense, [is permanently excluded].
Furthermore, one must not accept [them].
Since each is based on its own specific meaning, they do not contradict one another.
That is to say:
In this sutra, it is stated based on those who do not repent that one who commits the seven heinous offenses will not receive the precepts in this present life;
however, since the treatises maintain that there is also the principle of receiving the precepts through repentance, they omit this point.
Fourth, regarding the formal performance of the *karmavācanā*:
as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
from this point forward one should speak as follows.
"You, son of good family named [so-and-so],
wish to receive in succession from me all the training precepts of a bodhisattva and all the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva."
These are the so-called ethics of restraint,
the ethics of gathering virtuous dharmas,
and the ethics of benefiting sentient beings.
Such training rules and such pure precepts have already been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past.
All bodhisattvas of the future shall fully possess [these],
and all bodhisattvas currently present throughout the ten directions now fully possess these points of training.
Regarding this pure precept:
all bodhisattvas of the past have already studied it;
all bodhisattvas of the future shall study it.
All bodhisattvas of the present are now training in this.
Are you able to receive it? If you are able to receive it, [then do so].
The Bodhisattva who bestows [the precepts] spoke thus for the second and third times as well.
The Bodhisattva who receives [the precepts] likewise answered for the second and third times.
The Bodhisattva who bestows [the precepts] then asked this question.
When the third bestowal of the pure precepts has been completed,
the candidate who is receiving them responds in this manner;
this continues until the third request for witness.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:
"Having received the pure precepts,
one is able to receive the bodhisattva [vows] without rising from one's seat."
The Bodhisattva Capable of Bestowing, before an image of the Buddha,
universally pays homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas currently residing throughout the ten directions,
making offerings and prostrating at their feet.
He makes this formal announcement:
"The Bodhisattva named [Name],
has now [received the precepts] from me, the Bodhisattva [Name]."
Recite this up to three times to receive the bodhisattva precepts:
"I, [Name], a bodhisattva, have already received them with [Name] acting as witness.
I pray only that all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the foremost true sages within the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions..."
In all times and places, whether manifest or unmanifest,
may all sentient beings who are currently training as learners bear witness that [I], bearing this name, have received the bodhisattva precepts.
The second and third [recitations] were likewise.
When the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts was completed,
immediately thereafter:
Throughout all the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions, before the Buddhas currently residing therein and before the bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages,
this natural sign manifests as a matter of course.
This indicates that when a bodhisattva has thus received the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas,
at that time, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions [bear witness].
Thereupon, through the natural law of phenomena, mindfulness arises;
by means of that mindfulness,
right knowledge and vision proceed.
Through right knowledge and vision,
one realizes as it truly is that in a certain world there is a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name.
In the presence of such a bodhisattva,
one correctly receives the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas;
all [beings] regard this bodhisattva who has received the precepts as a son or a younger brother.
They give rise to thoughts of kinship and goodwill;
they cherish and have compassion for them.
It is through the cherishing and compassion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that this occurs.
It causes this bodhisattva’s pursuit of wholesome dharmas to increase all the more,
without any decline;
one should know that this is called the bodhisattva precept.
Thus, having requested the witness and performed the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) for receiving the bodhisattva precepts,
both the preceptor and the recipient together perform offerings.
He prostrates at the feet of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions and withdraws with reverence.
Such is the ethical discipline of restraint received by this bodhisattva.
Regarding all other observed vows and precepts,
this is the most excellent, unsurpassed, immeasurable, and boundless treasury of great merit that follows one;
it is the foremost and supreme.
To speak at length, up to and including all the prātimokṣa restraints,
[are included] within this bodhisattva restraint of morality.
A hundredth part does not equal it;
a thousandth part does not equal it;
even a numerical fraction does not equal it.
It does not amount to a fraction of a calculation;
it does not amount to a fraction of an arithmetic reckoning;
it does not amount to even a metaphorical fraction.
It does not even approach a fraction of the *upaniṣad* portion,
because it encompasses all great merits.
Second, the explanation of those who receive the precepts through a self-vow.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter forty:
"Furthermore, when bodhisattvas wish to receive the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),"
If one does not encounter a person endowed with complete merit,
then at that time one should personally receive the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline before an image of the Tathāgata.
One should receive it in this manner:
baring the right shoulder and placing the right knee upon the ground.
Or, squatting or kneeling,
he speaks thus: "I, who am named so-and-so."
I reverently address all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages.
I now wish, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, to...
I vow to undertake all the training precepts of a bodhisattva;
I vow to undertake all the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva,
namely, the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas and the precept of benefiting sentient beings—
such are the training rules.
Such pure ethical discipline has been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past and will be fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future.
All present bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions now fully possess such rules of training and such pure precepts.
All bodhisattvas of the past have already studied this;
all bodhisattvas of the future shall study it;
and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are studying it now.
The second and third [times] should also be spoken in this manner.
Having spoken, one should rise.
All the rest is as before.
It should be understood as before.
However, regarding self-administered [ordination],
one must first perform repentance.
One must necessarily obtain a favorable sign;
this shall serve as the limit.
If a favorable sign is not obtained, [the practice is not completed].
Because one has not obtained the precepts.
This sutra states below: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when one wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts with a sincere mind..."
Before an image of the Buddha,
one should make a vow to receive the precepts;
for seven days, one should repent before the Buddha until a favorable sign is seen.
One then obtains the precepts.
If a favorable sign is not obtained,
one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, seven weeks, or even up to a year.
One must obtain auspicious signs.
Having obtained auspicious signs,
one may then receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.
If one does not obtain a good sign,
even if one receives the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, one will not attain the precepts.
However, if one receives the precepts in the presence of a Dharma Master who has previously received the Bodhisattva precepts...
There is no need to see auspicious signs;
because this Dharma Master has received the transmission through a lineage of masters,
auspicious signs are unnecessary.
If there is no preceptor capable of conferring the precepts within a thousand li,
one may receive the precepts before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, provided that one obtains a favorable sign.
This is the sixth condition for relinquishing the precepts.
This further consists of two parts:
first, the conditions for obtaining the precepts;
second, the conditions for relinquishing the precepts.
There are further two kinds of conditions for obtaining the precepts:
first, the conditions for the seven classes of practitioners obtaining the precepts;
second, the conditions for a bodhisattva obtaining the precepts.
There are two aspects to the attainment of the precepts for the seven classes of followers:
first, the distinctions in the attainment of the precepts;
second, the conditions for possessing the precepts.
There are two ways of obtaining the precepts:
first, those who possess the full set of precepts;
second, the other six groups of practitioners.
Regarding those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*),
the various schools differ;
this applies to the other six groups as well.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
this is to manifest the ten types of non-restraint.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are ten ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The first is by nature (*svayaṃbhū*)."
Second, those who have seen the truth;
third, those who come with a welcome;
fourth, those who take the vow by themselves.
5. Discussion;
6. Receiving the weighty dharmas;
7. Sending a messenger.
The eight [precepts] are obtained by requesting with five virtues;
the ninth is obtained through the formal ritual (karmavācanā);
and there are thirteen returns.
Those who attain [enlightenment] spontaneously are the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Spontaneous" refers to wisdom that does not derive from a teacher;
at the moment one realizes this wisdom,
one attains full ordination.
Question:
Why is it not said that an Arhat naturally attains the precepts,
but only that a Pratyekabuddha does?
Answer:
Pratyekabuddhas, possessing sharp faculties, naturally attain the precepts;
because Arhats have dull faculties, the text does not mention them.
In this context, it refers exclusively to the great pratyekabuddhas and not to those who travel in groups.
Question:
Does this naturally acquired precept involve manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*)?
If there is no unmanifest action (avijñapti-karma),
how can it be said that the unmanifest arises apart from the manifest?
Answer:
Regarding the question, "What is the time of the informative [action] (*vijñapti*)?",
since there is no bodily or vocal informative action at the time of entering meditative insight (*samāpatti-jñāna*),
the answer is as follows:
When one enters meditative observation (dhyāna), at the moment this wisdom is attained,
it transforms into the fundamental [consciousness] capable of producing non-informative action (avijñapti).
Therefore, non-informative action also arises based upon informative action (vijñapti).
Question:
How is it known that one has attained the state of an Arhat?
There is no such thing as obtaining the precepts spontaneously.
Answer:
This is because there are śrāmaṇeras who are arhats, and so forth.
As it is said in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*:
"In the past, there were arhats and śrāmaṇeras in a monastery," and so forth,
as explained at length.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 23, states:
"These two śrāmaṇeras were both arhats liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
Therefore, it is known that [the precepts] cannot be obtained [in such cases].
Question:
Does one who attains the precepts spontaneously first obtain the five precepts and the ten precepts?
Answer: No.
At the moment one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one simultaneously and instantaneously obtains the five precepts and the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*),
because of their sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*). Some say:
One first obtains the five precepts and subsequently obtains the full precepts,
as they are like a ladder.
Question:
Why is it that bhikṣuṇīs do not attain [the fruits] spontaneously?
Answer:
Because their nature and conduct are inferior.
It is certain that one cannot attain the state of a Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha) or a Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha) while possessing a female body.
Regarding those who attain [the fruits] through the vision of the truths, as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* concerning the thirty-seven [factors of enlightenment]: [text follows].
By entering into the state of rightness and departure from birth—
namely,
the five bhikṣus who, through realizing the path of vision (darśanamārga), obtained full ordination.
Question:
For what reason do bhikṣuṇīs not receive the precepts upon attaining the Path of Vision?
Answer:
Because these women have many faults and are subject to much affliction,
they do not possess the attainment of precepts through the Path of Vision.
Question:
For what reason did the five men obtain the precepts upon seeing the truths,
while other bhikṣus did not?
Answer:
These five bhikṣus were present when the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma.
One first attains the path of seeing because the stability of the Dharma increases.
Question:
Why did the five [disciples] attain the Path first?
Answer:
Because of their original vows.
As the Blessed One has said:
"In a past life, I was a king who gave my own blood and vital energy as an offering to a rākṣasa."
He immediately made this vow:
"When I become a Buddha,
I shall first deliver these five people."
The five rākṣasas are these five bhikṣus of the present. Furthermore,
in the past, when the Bodhisattva was in the form of a great fish, these five men saw him first.
...and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding the attainment of the precepts through the "Welcome" (Svāgata) formula, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because the Buddha addressed them with "Come, Bhikṣu," those such as Elāpattra and others—
by the power of their original vows and through the Buddha’s majestic empowerment— [attained realization].
As stated in both the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* and the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
One thousand disciples of the three Kāśyapas and two hundred and fifty disciples of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana all received the precepts through the "Come,
monk" formula (*ehi-bhikṣu*).
Regarding those who obtain the precepts through self-vow,
as stated in the *Nyāya*:
"By accepting the Buddha as one's Great Teacher..."
That is to say:
Mahākāśyapa asked,
"For what reason do other people not obtain [the precepts] through self-vow?"
Answer:
Because their faith and understanding are slight.
As for those who attain it through debate:
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Skillfully answering questions refers to Sudāyin."
Furthermore, how was this?
At the age of eight,
he came to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked him,
"Where is your home?
He immediately replied:
In the three realms there is no home;
the Buddha knew his faculties were sharp,
even though he was not yet of age.
The Sangha shall confer it upon him;
it is not at the time of answering questions that one obtains full ordination.
Regarding those who receive the eight weighty dharmas,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"By reverently receiving the eight weighty dharmas."
That is to say,
Mahāprajāpatī was the first.
Question:
From whom did that Great Lord of Beings receive the profound Dharma?
Answer:
This was originally taught by the Buddha.
Ānanda taught it to Mahāgovinda,
who received the eight points of respect from Ānanda.
As stated in the Madhyama Āgama, Sūtra 28:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One..."
"Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of asceticism?
For this reason,
can a woman, within this true Dharma and Vinaya, go forth from the home life to study the Path?"
The World-Honored One said,
"Stop, stop, Ānanda!
Do not harbor such thoughts."
Ānanda, if women were to leave the home life within this Dharma,
it would cause this holy life (brahmacarya) not to endure for long.
"It is just as if there were a household with many women and few men;
would that household be able to flourish and prosper?
No, World-Honored One."
It is so, Ānanda. If women were to leave the household life to study the path within this Dharma, [it would lead to the shortening of the true Dharma].
This holy life will not endure for long,
Ānanda. It is just as with a field of rice or a field of barley.
Just as the growth of weeds inevitably ruins a field,
so too does a woman who leaves her home to study the Path.
"This will cause this holy life not to endure for long.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,"
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been greatly benefited by the World-Honored One. Why is this so?
World-Honored One,
after my mother passed away,
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī nurtured me with her own breast milk.
The World-Honored One spoke at length,
and so on, until the Buddha addressed Ānanda.
I shall now explain to you, daughter, the eight rules for honoring teachers.
That is to say, a woman must not transgress them; she should uphold them throughout her entire life.
What are the eight rules of respect for the teacher? Ānanda,
a bhikṣuṇī must receive full ordination from a bhikṣu.
Ānanda, I have established for women the first rule of respect toward the Teacher: a bhikṣuṇī should,
every half-month, [pay homage to the Saṃgha of bhikṣus].
Every half-month, one should request instruction and exhortation from a bhikṣu.
This is the second [duty] regarding the place of residence,
even if no bhikṣu is present there.
One shall not accept the summer retreat.
This is the third [precept]: when a bhikṣuṇī has completed the summer retreat, she must seek out [the presence of] the three matters—what was seen, heard, or suspected—from within both assemblies.
This is the fourth.
If the bhikṣus do not listen,
the bhikṣuṇīs will be unable to hear the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
If there are those who hear it,
they shall indeed hear it. This is the fifth, Ānanda.
A bhikṣuṇī must not speak of an offense committed by a bhikṣu;
a bhikṣu may speak of an offense committed by a bhikṣuṇī.
This is the sixth [rule].
Ānanda, if a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense,
she must perform the mānatva penance for fifteen days before both assemblies.
This, Ānanda, is the seventh [requirement] for a bhikṣuṇī to receive full ordination.
Even if one has reached a hundred years of age, one must still approach those who have recently received full ordination with a humble mind,
prostrating and serving them with reverence.
This is the eighth rule of respect for teachers.
At that time, when Ānanda was teaching the eight rules of respect for Mahāprajāpatī, he said:
Mahāprajāpatī received the eight weighty rules and thereby attained ordination.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If women had not been permitted to go forth and train in this True Dharma and Discipline, [the Saṅgha would have endured for a thousand years]."
The True Dharma was destined to remain for one thousand years;
now five hundred years have been lost,
and five hundred years remain.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, fascicle two, is likewise the same as this sutra.
The meaning intended here is that one obtains full ordination (*upasampadā*) at the time of receiving the eight rules.
As stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
Upāli asked Pāṭaliputra regarding the undertaking of the eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*).
This constitutes going forth and becoming a bhikṣuṇī.
The other nuns said:
He asked the Buddha, saying:
"One should perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) and threefold proclamation (*karmavācanā*) in the presence [of the assembly].
Question."
If that is so, since the community of nuns has not yet reached the required number,
how can those others obtain the precepts?
Answer:
As the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"For fourteen years prior [to the formal establishment of the order], women were ordained by means of counting;
for fourteen years thereafter, they were ordained through the ritual of *karmavācanā*."
Furthermore, those two [texts] state that the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion with three proclamations) was established eight years after his attainment of enlightenment.
Moreover, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs also attained it through the method of counting the dharmas.
Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"Full ordination is received through the teacher's dharma."
With the exception of Kautamī and five hundred women,
all others were not permitted to receive full ordination through the method of the teacher by means of a messenger;
as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
By means of sending a messenger;
that is, the nun Dharmadinnā.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
The courtesan Pañcālaśīrṣā wished to go to a forest hermitage to receive full ordination; however,
on the road, a band of thieves seized her along with the others.
When the woman heard this, she did not dare to go.

The Buddha permitted her to receive full ordination from afar; once the formal procedure (*dharmakarma*) had been completed among the assembly of Śrāmaṇerīs, the preceptor placed the candidate for ordination in one location and led the group of ten nuns to a forest hermitage (*araṇya*).
They prostrate at the feet of the assembly of monks.
The Bhikṣuṇī Karma-master then requests the formal act (*karmavācanā*) from the assembly of monks on behalf of the [candidate].
Once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed,
the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the instructors (*ācārya*), leading ten nuns, return to the original location.
They call the candidate for ordination and instruct her to prostrate at the feet of the assembly.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"A nun may receive the precepts by dispatching a messenger."
Among them was only one daughter,
whose countenance was so exceptionally distinguished that she was peerless in the world.
If one goes there, fearing that evil people might plunder them,
this is permitted by the Buddha;
if such circumstances arise at the present time, it is likewise so.
It is permissible to dispatch a messenger to receive the precepts and to request the five virtuous qualities.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"This is because the master of the Vinaya serves as the fifth person."
This refers to those who obtain [ordination] through the ritual (*karmavācanā*) in border regions.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"By means of a group of ten."
This refers to the central lands, where this [ordination] applies to both monks and nuns.
Within the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for nuns, there are ten members from each of the two assemblies.
As for the statement that there are "fifty," this is said according to the absolute minimum.
Whether it be many or more than that, there is no harm as long as it accords with reason.
Regarding those who obtain the three refuges,
the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
By means of the threefold recitation of refuge in the Buddha, Dharma,
and Saṅgha— namely, when the sixty virtuous groups gathered together to receive full ordination.
The commentary explains:
The Buddha dispatched those beyond training (aśaikṣa) to preach the Three Refuges, whereby they immediately attained full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states:
The Buddha addressed Kauṇḍinya:
If there is one who has gone forth from the household life,
they shall shave off their hair and beard and be instructed with these words:
I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for as long as my life shall last.
I now go forth under the Buddha;
the Bhagavān is my teacher.
The ordination by means of the three statements is to be understood as I have explained.
The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya traveled to the country of Vaiśālī and subsequently arrived at the country of Vaiśālī.
In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there were people from the Vṛji clan;
two noble sons from these two clans lived together in one place.
All these people conceived this thought:
Ājñātakauṇḍinya has gone forth within the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa and practices the holy life.
After we had discussed the Dharma regarding his renunciation and training together,
we immediately went with one another to the place where Kauṇḍinya was,
prostrated ourselves at his feet, and paid him homage.
They addressed the Venerable One, saying,
"We pray only that the Great Virtuous One will grant us permission to go forth in the Dharma of the Tathāgata and practice the holy life.
Ājñātakauṇḍinya granted them permission to go forth.
He taught him the ordination by means of the three utterances.
Having received the precepts, they went together to where the Buddha was.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
If these sons of good family seek to go forth and receive the threefold formula for ordination,
will they obtain the precepts or not?
The Buddha told Kauṇḍinya:
"These people have properly received the precepts through the threefold formula."
Question:
For what reason do other persons not obtain full ordination through the three refuges?
Answer:
Before the rules were established, there was full ordination by means of three utterances;
after the World-Honored One established the rules, there was no longer full ordination by means of three utterances.
This was because a sick bhikṣu had no one to attend to him.
They went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the formal act (karmavācanā) consisting of three utterances is abolished."
Among the ten types of *saṃgha*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal motion with three proclamations) permits one to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Nyāyānusāra*, and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* all state that there are ten ways of obtaining the precepts;
this is identical to the ten ways of obtaining the precepts found in the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*.
First, the spontaneous;
second, the realization of the truths;
third, the question-and-answer.
Fourth, the three refuges;
fifth, the self-vow,
namely that of Mahākāśyapa.
The six groups of five,
the group of seven,
and the eightfold set of eight dharmas.
Ninth, dispatching messengers;
twelfth, the twelve divisions [of the scriptures],
namely the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Āgata* (Welcome), and the *Svāgata* (Well-Come).

Because he wished to proclaim the light of the precepts,
he emitted light from his mouth.
There are four causes and conditions for this.
For this reason, light is emitted:
first, to illuminate the suffering of sentient beings;
second, to produce a sense of rarity and wonder.
Third, it evokes conditions for existence;
fourth, it extinguishes the darkness of birth and death. Sūtra.
"At that time, there were one hundred trillion great kings. The commentary states:
"There are two types of assemblies for the fourth [assembly]:
first, the initial gathering of the assembly."
Afterwards, they listen to the Dharma;
this constitutes the assembly.
There are five ways in which the assembly gathers.
First, the miscellaneous assembly, such as the great multitude of hundreds of billions;
second, the assembly of bodhisattvas;
third, the assembly of Brahmās.
Fourth, the assembly of the six heavens of the desire realm;
fifth, the assembly of kings.
As for what is called the Brahmā heaven:
The first dhyāna consists of three heavens:
first, the Brahmakāyika Heaven;
second, the Brahmapurohita Heaven.
The three Brahmā heavens:
within the second dhyāna stage, there are three heavens;
the first is Parīttābha (Limited Light).
Second is the Heaven of Immeasurable Light;
third is the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Radiance.
Within the station of the Third Dhyāna, there are three heavens.
First, the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven;
second, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven;
third, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
In the fourth dhyāna stage, there are nine heavens:
first, the Anabhraka Heaven;
second, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven.
Third, the Heaven of Vast Results;
fourth, the Heaven of Non-conceptual Sentient Beings;
and fifth, the five Pure Abodes.
The five Pure Abodes are:
first, the Heaven of No Affliction;
second, the Heaven of No Heat.
Third, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven;
fourth, the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven;
fifth, the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
Beyond these Śuddhāvāsa deities, there is the Mahāmaheśvara heaven.
Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are born in that heaven, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Twenty-one [Sthānas]), which says: "In the *Yogācāra-bhūmi*, it is said: [and so forth].
It is called "Brahma" because it is produced from extensive goodness (*kuśala*).
Since this Brahma is great, he is called Mahābrahmā.
This is because he has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Because it arises first,
because it passes away last,
and because its majestic power and other qualities are superior.
He is named Mahābrahmā.
Those who are his emanations and subjects are called the Brahma-pārṣadyas (the Retinue of Brahmā).
Because they stand in front of Mahābrahmā and serve as his attendants, they are called the Brahma-purohitās (the Ministers of Brahmā).
Within the devas of their own stage, the radiance is the smallest, and is thus called "Limited Light" (Parīttābha).
Because the radiance becomes increasingly superior and its measure is difficult to fathom, it is called "Immeasurable Light" (Apramāṇābha).
Because pure light shines everywhere throughout the region of their own stage, it is called "Utmost Light" (Ābhāsvara).
The pleasant sensation of the stage of pure mind is called "pure.
Because this purity is minimal and inferior within its own stage, it is called "limited purity" (parītta-śubha).
Because this purity increases further until its measure becomes difficult to fathom, it is called "immeasurable purity" (apramāṇa-śubha).
Because this purity is all-pervasive, it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna).
Since the ground where the gods dwell in the lower space is like clouds closely joined together, it is called "Cloud" (Abhra);
above these gods, there is no further ground of clouds.
Because there is no "cloud-head" (anabhraka) there, it is called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka).
Because one must possess further superior merit as an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) to be reborn there, it is named "Merit-born" (Puṇyaprasava).
Because this is the most excellent among the fruits of ordinary beings, it is called "Vast Fruit" (Bṛhatphala).
The noble ones who have abandoned desire are called "pure" because they wash away the defilements of affliction with the water of the Noble Path.
Because they dwell in these pure bodies, they are called the "Pure Abodes.
"Prolixity" refers to being cluttered and mixed.
Some say it is called "prolix" (*apramāṇa*) because it is the first among the heavens that lack prolixity;
others say it is called "without prolixity" (*apramāṇa*) because it is the most inferior among the heavens.
Having already skillfully subdued and eliminated the superior and middling grades of obstacles to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
Because his intentions are harmonious and supple,
and he is free from all afflictions and fevers,
it is called "Without Heat" (Atapa).
Alternatively, that which causes the arising of afflictions below is called "heat.
By being initially free from this, one attains the name "without heat" (*an-uṣṇa*).
Having thus attained the superior grade (*adhimātra*), [one proceeds].
Because the fruits and virtues of his mixed cultivation of dhyāna are easily manifested,
he is named Sudarśana (Well-Apparent).
The hindrances to meditative concentration have been mixed and refined;
other categories have become extremely subtle,
and vision is utterly clear and penetrating.
Therefore it is named Sudarśana (Good to Behold).
There is no other place where one can surpass this within the realm of form.
It is called the ultimate limit of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-paryanta*).

Alternatively, because this has reached the final boundary of the body which is the basis for all suffering, it is called the ultimate limit of name-and-form, as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 21, regarding the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage.
Fully endowed with supernormal powers,
they exercise mastery over their transformations and encounter no obstruction regarding their objects.
He is named Maheśvara.
As for the six heavens of the desire realm:
first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājika).
2. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; 3.
The Yāma Heaven (translated here as "Time-Portion"); 4. The Tuṣita Heaven (translated here as "Contentment"); 5. The Nirmāṇarati Heaven (translated here as "Delight in Emanation");
6. The Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven.
Each point should be understood as explained in the treatise (*śāstra*).
Regarding the sixteen great kingdoms,
it is as stated in the fifth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*:
First, the kingdom of Aṅga;
second, the kingdom of Magadha;
third, the kingdom of Kāśī; fourth, the kingdom of Kośala.
5. The country of Vajji;
6. The country of Malla;
7. The country of Cetiya.
8. The country of Bāṣpa;
9. The country of Kuru;
10. The country of Kajaṅgala.
11. The country of Aśmaka;
12. The country of Cañcā;
13. The country of Sālāṭa.
14. The country of Gandhāra;
15. The country of Kamboja;
16. The country of Arista.
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 125, states:
"The sixteen great kingdoms are as follows:
the kingdom of Aṅga..."
The kingdom of Magadha,
the kingdom of Kāśī,
and the kingdom of Kośala.
The country of Pṛṣṭhī,
the country of Malla,
and the country of Puṇḍra.
The country of Sukṣma;
the country of Arbuda;
the country of Arbudi.
The country of Yavadvīpa,
the country of Kamboja,
and the country of Kuru.
The country of Pañcāla,
the country of Vatsa,
and the country of Śroṇāparāntaka.
[Sūtra]:
"With palms joined and a sincere mind, one should abide in the precepts. [Commentary]:
This is the second [point], listening to the Dharma.
[Sūtra]:
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "...down to reciting the Buddha’s Dharma and precepts for oneself. [Commentary]:
The second part, the correct explanation of the characteristics of the precepts, has two sections.
First, a brief praise and exhortation to uphold [the precepts];
second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the formal explanation of the characteristics of the precepts.
Within the former, there are two parts.
First, a brief praise and exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively" onwards, the instruction regarding the capacity of those to be reached.
Within the former, there are three parts.
First, the exhortation to recite;
second, the praise of virtues;
third, from "Therefore, the great assembly... onwards, the conclusion of the exhortation to recite and uphold.
The preceding section has two parts;
this is the first, which reveals the Buddha’s own recitation.
That is to say, the Blessed One recalled a past thought.
Therefore, it is constantly recited;
furthermore, because it benefits others,
one recites it oneself.
Sūtra: "You all should also recite this. Commentary:
The second [point] is the exhortation to others to recite.
The "first arousal of the mind" refers to the ten stages of faith.
The "ten stages of setting forth" refers to...
This means that in the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*), one resolutely sets out and never regresses;
this is termed "setting out.
As stated in the aforementioned sutra.
O Buddhas, you should know that within the stage of firm faith and receptivity (*adhimukti-kṣānti*), there are ten minds directed toward the fruit of the stages of departure (*niryāṇa-citta*).
First, the mind of relinquishment;
second, the mind of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Third, the mind of patience;
fourth, the mind of diligence;
fifth, the mind of concentration.
Sixth, the mind of wisdom;
seventh, the mind of aspiration;
eighth, the mind of protection.
Ninth, the mind of joy;
tenth, the summit mind.
Regarding the ten nurtured minds:
This refers to cultivating the emptiness of phenomena during the stage of the ten practices,
thereby nourishing the categories of wholesome qualities,
as explained in the aforementioned sutra.
O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten stages of entering the firmness of various patiences, there arise ten ways of nurturing the mind toward the fruit:
first, a mind of loving-kindness.
Second, the mind of compassion;
third, the mind of sympathetic joy;
fourth, the mind of equanimity.
5. The mind of giving;
6. The mind of kind speech;
7. The mind of benefit.
8. The mind of sameness;
9. The mind of concentration;
10. The mind of wisdom.
The ten adamantine minds refer to those within the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*),
as explained in the aforementioned sutra.
From the ten developmental minds (*puṣṭi-citta*), one enters the firm cultivation of patience (*kṣānti*); from among the ten adamantine minds (*vajra-citta*) directed toward the fruit, there are:
first, the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*); second, the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti-citta*).
Third, the profound mind;
fourth, the penetrating mind;
fifth, the straightforward mind.
Sixth, the mind of non-retrogression;
seventh, the Mahāyāna mind;
eighth, the signless mind.
Ninth, the mind of ninefold benefit;
tenth, the indestructible mind.
O Buddhas, you should know this.
From these ten adamantine minds, one enters the stage of firm noble patience (*āryakṣānti*), wherein the fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are realized:
first, the stage of the equality of essential nature;
second, the stage of excellent wisdom of essential nature.
Third, the stage of the luminosity of intrinsic nature;
fourth, the stage of intrinsic nature as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*);
fifth, the stage of the wisdom-illumination of intrinsic nature.
Sixth is the Ground of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature;
seventh is the Ground of Fulfillment of Essential Nature;
eighth is the Ground of the Buddha’s Roar of Essential Nature.
The ninth is the stage of the Flower-Adornment of Essential Nature;
the tenth is the stage of Entering the Buddha’s Realm of Essential Nature.
Regarding the first of these ten stages of advancement, it is the mind of equanimity.
One renounces all kingdoms, cities, towns, fields, houses, gold, silver, bright jewels, sons, daughters, one’s own body, and all conditioned things.
One renounces everything—those that are unconditioned and signless, as well as the false aggregations of self, person, knowledge, and views.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the precepts and the mind:

O Sons of the Buddha, if the precepts were not non-precepts, there would be no one who receives them; the ten wholesome precepts would have no teacher, and there would be no preaching of the Dharma, only deception and theft.
Even up to wrong views, there is no accumulation [of them] for those who possess compassion, kindness, rectitude, truthfulness, right view, equanimity, and joy.
These ten constitute the essence of the precepts, which restrain the mind from the eight inversions.
All natures are detached; this is the single path of purity.
As for the one with a patient mind, O Buddha-sons, it is the essence of signless generosity.
It endures all things throughout the entirety of empty space;
this endurance is called the practice of endurance of non-arising.
"It is designated as such in all instances, just as with the patience regarding suffering," and so forth,
as explained at length.
As for "the advancing mind":
O disciples of the Buddha,
whether engaged in the four modes of deportment or at all times,
one should practice by conforming to emptiness, relying on the provisional, and uniting with the dharma-nature.
Regarding the concentrated mind:
O disciples of the Buddha,
it is the samādhi of immeasurable mind through the practice of quiescence and signlessness.
Whether ordinary beings or noble ones, there are none who do not enter samādhi;
their essential natures are in accord,
all by virtue of the power of meditative concentration.
The nature of all views regarding self, person, agent, and experiencer is subject to transformation.

These are the causes and conditions of obstruction; like a scattering wind that agitates the mind, one should use still wisdom to contemplate that all things are merely designated as provisional combinations.
This is explained at length.
Regarding "the mind of wisdom":
O sons of the Buddha, the essence of wisdom that is empty is not a cognition devoid of conditions; it is called the mind that discriminates all dharmas as provisional names.
Up to and including taking wisdom as the foremost,
one cultivates ineffable contemplative wisdom to enter the Middle Way of the Single Truth.
As for the aspirational mind:
If a disciple of the Buddha wishes for greatness and seeks all things:
"seeking greatness" refers to seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and equal great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*);
"seeking all things" refers to seeking all practices (*sarva-caryā*).
Regarding the "guarding of the mind":

if a disciple of the Buddha is defiled by the three jewels, it will cause all the merits of their practice to be corrupted, such that the eight inversions and evil views of non-Buddhists do not disturb their right faith, and they extinguish the fetters of the self-view and the fetters of views.
As for the mind of joy (*muditā-citta*):
if a disciple of the Buddha sees others obtain happiness, they should always give rise to joy.
As for the mind of the crown (*mūrdha-citta*): [it is as follows].
If a disciple of the Buddha possesses this supreme wisdom, they extinguish the wheel of the view of self.
Herein, "supreme wisdom" refers to the wisdom of non-self, because it extinguishes the view of self.
All views are thereby brought to stillness and extinction.
Twenty: Nurturing through a compassionate mind.
If a disciple of the Buddha constantly practices a compassionate mind, having already produced the causes for happiness, then...
One contemplates in accordance with the joy of the wisdom of selflessness,

entering into all great dharmas— such as sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and form (*rūpa*)— wherein they are without arising and without abiding;
this is explained at length.

In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) consists of the mental attention directed toward a mind associated with happiness, because one desires to bestow happiness upon sentient beings who lack it. Compassion (*karuṇā*),
on the other hand, is as follows:
If a Buddha’s disciple, through compassion, emptiness, and signlessness, practices the path with compassionate understanding,
they shall personally extinguish all suffering and give rise to equal wisdom regarding the immeasurable sufferings of all sentient beings.
In this context, compassion extracts the suffering of sentient beings.
Through great compassion that takes no object (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), one cultivates a mind of equanimity toward all— enemies, friends, and neutral parties—
and delivers them from their various sufferings.
Regarding the mind of joy:
O Son of the Buddha, when one experiences the joyful mind of non-arising, the essence and characteristics of the lineage, the wisdom of the path, and the emptiness of emptiness do not cling to "mine.
One rejoices in all sentient beings, gives rise to emptiness, enters the path, abandons evil associates, and seeks out virtuous friends.
Show us the good path so that all sentient beings may enter the home of the Buddha-dharma;
they should give rise to joy and enter the stage of the Dharma.
Regarding the mind of equanimity:
one should give rise to the mind of equanimity within the unconditioned, signless, and empty dharmas.

Just as the numinous void is equal toward both seeing and not seeing, and toward the two—sin and merit, good and evil—it illuminates with a single light that which is neither person nor "mine," such that the essential natures of self and other cannot be established; this is great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
Even to the point of sacrificing one's own blood, limbs, and hands, one should practice the mind of relinquishment without generating any thought of attachment.
One who cultivates this mind of giving can guide all sentient beings by means of the gift of material wealth, the gift of the Dharma, and the gift of spiritual instruction.
The internal body, the external body, kingdoms, cities, men, women, fields, and houses are all the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).

As for "the speech of the mind," it refers to entering the samādhi of loving speech (*priyavāditā*) through its essential nature; it is the discourse on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), true speech, and unified speech that harmonizes all sentient beings and gives rise to their roots of goodness.
The mind of benefit refers to observing that those before whom one practices the seven riches obtain profit; thus,
one sustains the body and life and enters the samādhi of benefit, manifesting all forms of body, speech, and mind.
"Those of one mind" means that,
through the Dharma, they share the nature of the Way, delight in the kalpas as being identical to emptiness within the dharma of non-arising,
and through the wisdom of non-self, they are born together in non-duality.
Yet, manifesting immeasurable bodies according to the various types of beings, one enters all matters within the six realms of existence with complete identity.

As for "the concentrated mind," it means that when the mind is still, it takes my own dharmas as its object; because the mind moves, turns, and fluctuates through the favorable and unfavorable, the entering and exiting, one should enter the hundred samādhis.

"Beneficent mind" refers to the contemplation that the afflictions of false views and fetters, being subject to transformation, lack a determinate intrinsic nature; because they accord with the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*), they are identical to emptiness.
Thus, this mind enters the path of the emptiness of emptiness and gives rise to the mind of non-arising (*anutpāda-citta*).
The thirtieth is the adamantine mind of faith.
Regarding "faith":
it means that among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), faith is the foremost.
The root of all virtues:
not giving rise to the heterodox views of non-Buddhists,
and not forming karmic bonds through the creation of conditioned existence.
The mind does not undergo reception;
because the mind is empty, its successive faiths are quiescent, which is called the "faith of non-belief.
As for the mindful mind:
That is to say, one should practice the six recollections:

one should recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, the devas, and generosity; and one should recollect the ultimate truth, emptiness, non-attachment, and non-liberation, dedicating these toward the wisdom that enters the dharma-realm.
The profound mind refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the wisdom that illuminates the emptiness of real phenomena, there is the existence of the true reality (*satya*);
this middle way within dependent origination is called the true reality.
The provisional designations of all phenomena— such as self, person, and master— are called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Within these two truths, one enters deeply into emptiness and attains profound liberation.
The "one who has attained penetration" refers to one who,
through the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*), realizes that the true nature of all things is neither bound nor liberated and is entirely empty.
This emptiness is called the penetration of the emptiness of all phenomena.
The "straight mind" directly perceives and grasps the conditions of the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) and enters the wisdom of non-arising.
It teaches and transforms all sentient beings, turning them all toward the emptiness of *sarvajñā* (omniscience), which is the direct, true nature. "Straight" means correct.
One who possesses the non-retrogressive mind does not enter the stage of any ordinary person and does not give rise to new or nurtured views.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to the karma of entering the three realms through the semblance of a self or persons based on habitual causes;
for those who possess the mind of the Mahāyāna alone are liberated into the single emptiness.
The mind of all conditioned phenomena is called the "single vehicle" (ekayāna); by employing it as its primary function,
one crosses the river of the three realms and enters the ocean of Buddhahood.
Regarding "non-conceptualization":
it is the liberation from false conceptualization that illuminates the non-duality of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
All fetters, karmic activities, and the phenomena of the three periods of time are suchness (*tathatā*).
Because all things are likewise unarisen and empty,
they are signless in mind.
As for "suchness-wisdom," it refers to the immeasurable dharma-realm, which is without accumulation or reception, and wherein birth after birth is free from afflictions.
Furthermore, all dharma-gates, the path practiced by all worthies, and all dharmas contemplated by all sages—whatever they may be—are likewise so.
All the teachings, skillful means, dharmas, and meanings of the Buddha’s instruction are gathered within his mind.
One whose mind is indestructible enters the wisdom of the noble stages,

draws near to liberation, attains the true gateway to the Path, clarifies the bodhicitta, subdues through patience, accords with emptiness, remains unshaken by the eight māras, and receives the crowning touch of the hands of all the sages.
The Buddhas exhort and inspire him to enter the Samādhi of the Hand-Placement upon the Crown;
emitting light from his body, he illumines the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, entering the majestic spirit of the Buddhas with mastery over appearance and disappearance.
This is the fortieth stage.
The stage of the equality of essential nature refers to the true Dharma transforming all flowers of practice, fulfilling the fruits of the four heavens, and abiding in the pure land of the Buddhas;
it is the birth into the family of the Buddhas through immeasurable great vows, eloquence, and fearlessness, and the sitting upon the ground of the Buddha-nature.
Having ultimately ceased to undergo the causes and effects of ordinary beings due to all obstacles, they experience great bliss and joy;
they enter immeasurable Buddha-lands from a single Buddha-land,
and enter immeasurable eons from a single eon.
...and so forth, as extensively explained.
Regarding the stage of the nature of wholesome wisdom (*kuśala-prajñā-svabhāva-bhūmi*):
it refers to the pure and clear penetration of all roots of goodness (*sarva-kuśalamūla*).
That which is called "loving-kindness, relinquishment, and the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths" refers to delivering sentient beings from suffering.
As for the "ground of luminous essence," it means knowing all dharma-gates of the three periods of time through the wisdom that understands by means of samādhi.
Regarding what are called the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*):
it refers to the total retention (*dhāraṇī*), eloquence (*pratibhāna*), the mind and mental activities being empty (*citta-cittacaitta-śūnyatā*), and so forth, as explained at length.
As for the stage of the nature of reality (*dharmatā-bhūmi*): [it is as follows].
That is to say, by practicing the factors of enlightenment through the non-interruption and non-permanence of both the ultimate and conventional truths,
one enters into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform all sentient beings,
causing them to perceive the Buddha-nature as eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
Regarding "the ground of the essence-nature’s illuminating wisdom":
it means that within this ground, the category of the ten powers (*daśabala*) arises as all meritorious practices.
Regarding "the flower-light of the essence-nature": [it refers to...]
The stages are as explained in the aforementioned sutra.
Within the category of the ten supernormal powers and clear wisdom regarding all worlds, one displays various transformations to all sentient beings;

through the clear wisdom of the divine eye, one knows all forms—down to the atoms within the lands of the three periods of time—and distinguishes them according to their division into the six realms of existence.
By means of the wisdom of the divine ear, one knows the sounds of suffering and joy of sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
By means of the wisdom of the divine body, one knows all forms, whether material or immaterial, and neither male nor female.
Within a single thought-moment, he manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms in the lands and eons of the ten directions and the three periods of time;
with the divine knowledge of others' minds, he knows the conduct of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
By means of the knowledge of devas and humans, they know the past lives of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time;
by means of the knowledge of liberation, they know the liberation of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Having severed all afflictions, whether many or few,
he uses the supernormal knowledge of the mind of devas to know the settled or unsettled minds of sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
By means of celestial awakening-wisdom, one knows whether all sentient beings have already attained Buddhahood or have not yet attained it;
one knows the teachings being expounded within the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of celestial mindfulness-wisdom, one knows the duration of the lifespans of all sentient beings throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas.
By means of the wisdom of celestial vows, he knows the ten stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) for all sentient beings—
the stages in which each and every practice and vow reaches fulfillment within the thirty mental states—
and specifically the stage of the eighteen categories of noble wisdom, which is not shared with those of the lower stages.
The "wisdom portion of the eighteen unique qualities" refers to the nature of the Buddha’s Lion’s Roar stage,
which is the samādhi of entering the rank of the Dharma King.
Because his wisdom knows the Buddha-Buddha-Roar Samādhi,
the practice of the Great Illumination Samādhi is constantly present before him;
he can thus bestow the medicine of the Dharma upon all sentient beings.
Acting as a great Dharma Master, he destroys the four māras;
his Dharma-body manifests through emanations, entering the realm of the Buddhas;
his essential nature is the stage of the Avataṃsaka.
As the Sūtra says:

"By means of the Buddha’s majestic demeanor and the Tathāgata’s Samādhirāja-samādhi, he enters and emerges from meditative absorption at no fixed time, simultaneously attaining Buddhahood and turning the wheel of Dharma throughout ten billion sets of four continents within the worlds of the ten directions."
Regarding "the essential nature entering the stage of the Buddha-realm":
this means that his great wisdom is empty, empty again, and even further empty.
Because his equalizing wisdom is like space and identical to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), he is called the Tathāgata.
At that time, they were born upon jeweled lotus flowers;
all were granted the prediction of enlightenment,
and the Dharma-body Hand, filled with joy, stroked their crowns.
The Bodhisattvas, who share the same views and the same practice, praise [the Buddha] with one voice and without duality.

Sūtra: "Therefore, the light of the precepts reaches [all places]; it is not without cause that there is light. Commentary: [This means that] because the light of the precepts is present, it is not without cause that light appears.
The second part, the praise of virtues, has three sections:
first, the discernment of the superior causes;
second, the elimination of characteristics, beginning with "the light is not blue, etc."; and third, [the elimination of characteristics] through the absence of increase and decrease.
Third, regarding the source of all Buddhas, the following praises its function.
This constitutes the first section, which distinguishes the supreme cause.
As for the term "light of precepts":

Because they are able to rescue and protect sentient beings who have no protector,
they are called "rescuers and protectors. As for those who have no protector:
This means they are solitary.
As the fifth fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In this state, there is no one to provide rescue."
Because of being solitary and alone,
one is without rescue;
there are nine types of such metaphors.
First, they are perpetually impoverished, solitary, and without refuge.
Second, the fires of the three poisons blaze incessantly, leaving them solitary and without refuge.
Third, they are confined within the firm prison of the three realms of existence, solitary and without refuge.
Fourth, they will be shrouded by the dense forests of afflictions, solitary and without refuge.
Fifth, lacking the power of right contemplation, they will be solitary and without refuge.
Sixth, being far removed from wholesome dharmas and devoid of joy and happiness in their minds, they will be solitary and without refuge.
Seventh, they lose the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas and are solitary and without rescue.
Eighth, they constantly follow the worldly stream and are solitary and without rescue.
Ninth, they lose the skillful means for nirvāṇa and are solitary and without rescue.

Question: How much merit is there in a single moment of the impure precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*) of a bodhisattva?
Answer:
The pure precepts of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (*prathama-bodhicittotpādaka*), in a single moment...
It surpasses the pure precepts of all those of the two vehicles,
let alone others.
As stated in the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, fascicle 586:
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
suppose all sentient beings in the world were to accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action;
whatever precepts they possess—
Compared to the single instance of bodhisattva precepts at the time of the initial resolve among the assembly of bodhisattvas who have generated the mind for unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment, [the former] does not equal even one hundredth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part.
The detailed exposition continues until Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asks Śāriputra:
"What is the bodhisattva’s impure pure morality?"
Seeking only their own benefit and dedicating [merit] toward nirvāṇa,
whereas the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva is universally for the sake of liberating immeasurable sentient beings.
Dedicating it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva thus surpasses the untainted pure ethical discipline of the two vehicles.
In this regard, one should diligently guard the precept against killing with a focused mind,
as stated in the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), fascicle 15.
This is for the sake of upholding the precepts.
He did not spare his own body or life in order to protect the pure precepts, just like a single *srotāpanna*.
There was once a man born into a family of butchers who was approaching adulthood.
He ought to attend to his family business,
yet he is unwilling to kill.
His parents placed a knife and a sheep inside a room and spoke to him, saying:
"If you do not kill this sheep, you shall not be allowed to go out and see the light of the sun and moon.
The son thought to himself:
"If I kill this one sheep..."
Thinking, "I shall surely end my life by this very act;
how could I commit such a great sin for the sake of my own body," he then took a knife and committed suicide.
The parents opened the door and saw the sheep standing on one side;
the child had already passed away.
At the very moment he took his own life, he was reborn in the heavens.
